item.title: IMF/World Bank meetings leave developing countries with more questions than answers
item.description: Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble.
item.dc:creator: Andrea Shalal, David Lawder
item.content:encoded: Last week's meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank yielded no new answers for the developing world to the questions posed by a spreading Middle East war, continuing war in Ukraine, rising debt payments and a potential AI bubble. Not for the first time, [USN:L1N46302K TEXT:"lower-income countries"] are being rocked by the spillover from the actions of wealthier nations: rising debt service costs, higher inflation and the risk of falling ever further behind economically thanks to the AI boom. What they got was the stock advice the global lenders always dish out: to shrink fiscal deficits and accelerate economic reforms to attract more private sector investment. Kristalina Georgieva, the first IMF chief from a developing nation - Bulgaria - said advanced economies were in fact the worst offenders on budget imbalances. She noted that developing countries' debt levels had actually fallen in recent years, only for surging bond yields elsewhere to drive up their borrowing costs. Average debt service payments there had more than doubled from a decade ago to 14% of government revenue, crowding out education, healthcare and other critical areas, she said. ADVANCED ECONOMIES FOCUSED ON THEIR OWN PROBLEMS At a panel on Saturday, Georgieva said many issues remained unresolved, especially around AI: "We are in a place where we have many more questions than we have answers. And my alert to everybody is: Do not fall for the guys that pretend they have the answers. They are tricking you." Josh Lipsky, vice president of international economics at the Atlantic Council think tank, said the meetings had flunked their opportunity to come up with guidance or ways to help. "It's hard to talk about the developing world when the advanced economies don't have their act together and are at risk of a fiscal crisis," he said. "And that's on top of political situations in many of these countries that makes development aid not a priority at the moment." Mauricio Cardenas, Colombia's former finance minister and now a research scholar at Columbia University's School of International and Public Affairs in New York, said many policymakers were left with a deep sense that "something really bad could happen" but no real roadmap to navigate the future. "The IMF and World Bank are not particularly well prepared for this new phase. They understand that something is going on, they bring in experts on AI," he said. "But in the end, there's no kind of specific, concrete advice on how to be prepared for something where you don't really understand how it's going to unfold." The geopolitical tensions that have roiled both institutions since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 - complicating concerted action - were also evident in Bangkok when nearly half the delegates at an [USN:L1N46301V TEXT:"IMF steering committee"] walked out when Russia's finance minister spoke. Houthi attacks on Riyadh airport delayed the arrival of the head of that committee, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, who had to travel overland to Qatar to catch a flight. And Bangkok itself was a stark reminder of the challenges facing developing countries, still partly under water after floods in September that caused almost $200 million in damage to Thailand's industrial sector. RISING INEQUALITY COULD RAISE COSTS IN LONG TERM Kate Pickett, a professor at the University of York, urged policymakers to focus on more inclusive growth rather than forcing developing countries into tough structural reforms. "If inequality increases, if poverty deepens, that will increase their costs in the long term," she said. "It's not enough to describe an economy as resilient. It's only resilient for the rich and the privileged.” Ayhan Kose, deputy chief economist at the World Bank, said the global economy had weathered its biggest energy shock - from the US-Israeli war on Iran - better than expected. But while a global recession had been avoided, he said growth outlooks in both developing and advanced economies were worse than before. Growth had already fallen off in half of advanced economies, while in developing countries as a whole, it had slowed significantly to around 3.6% from 4.4%. “People are really worried because resilience today is not a guarantee for resilience tomorrow," he said. "Now they are worried about what will be the next shock, because every six months, if not every three months, there is a new shock." While no specific initiatives were announced, he said the World Bank remained focused on helping developing countries prepare for advancements in AI, in part by mobilising more private capital, now at triple the levels of 2022. Yet it, too, has to contend with sharp drops in official development aid and persistent challenges in attracting foreign investment to developing countries. “The reality on the ground is the reality on the ground,” he said.

item.title: Iran urges US to accept proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
item.description: Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Iran's offer to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days is still on the table, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told Iranian media outlets on Sunday. Iran presented its proposal in mid-September after an [USN:L1N42P0Q6 TEXT:"interim ceasefire"] collapsed. Tehran later acknowledged receiving a US response but [USN:L1N45X04L TEXT:"Iran’s security chief"] said last week negotiations have stalled because Washington failed to address all [USN:L1N45Q01J TEXT:"seven conditions"] for reopening the strait. "Our situation is clear and based on the seven-days proposal presented to the US. They shared comments which we are reviewing, but our proposal is still on the table and if there is any honesty on the US part, which there isn't, the way to reopening the Strait of Hormuz is obvious," Araqchi said while in Baghdad for a meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Iran's conditions include, among other demands, the lifting of the US blockade on its ports, the lifting of US sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts. If Washington accepts Tehran's conditions, the strait could reopen within six days, with talks resuming the following day, Araqchi said. A central point of disagreement has been Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran's [USN:L1N45T0JD TEXT:"nuclear programme"] from the outset. US Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries' eight-month war. Tehran says negotiations should initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried about a fifth of the global trade in oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and restoring security in the waterway.

item.title: Accenture looks to sell Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, FT reports
item.description: IT consulting firm Accenture is looking to sell its Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: IT consulting firm Accenture (ACN.N) is looking to sell its Chinese operations for up to $1.5 billion, the Financial Times reported on Sunday, citing people familiar with the matter. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Accenture has hired JPMorgan (JPM.N) to work on a strategic review of the China business after receiving unsolicited interest in the unit over the past year, the report added. Accenture and JPMorgan did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment outside regular business hours. The sale process is likely to draw interest from private equity groups and a small cluster of strategic buyers, the report said. Accenture may opt to retain a significant minority stake in the business, the report added. Accenture’s Greater China operations include Taiwan, Hong Kong and mainland China, according to its website. The consultancy firm recently forecast full-year 2027 revenue growth between 3% and 6%, above analysts' estimates.

item.title: Pope Leo pledges gradual return to duties in first event since cancer surgery
item.description: Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago.
item.dc:creator: Joshua McElwee
item.content:encoded: Pope Leo pledged on Sunday to slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics as he greeted crowds in St. Peter's Square during his first public event since undergoing surgery for lung cancer five days ago. The 71-year-old pontiff had an [USN:S8N42Y05U TEXT:"operation"] on Tuesday to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, [USN:L8N4600P9 TEXT:"fuelling speculation"] about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy. Smiling from a window of the Vatican's Apostolic Palace as he spoke to pilgrims below in a firm, clear voice on Sunday, the first US pope thanked people across the world for their prayers and said he would now begin to resume his normal schedule. "Having overcome this delicate phase... I will now gradually resume my activities, always with the help of God and your prayers," Leo said. The pope, who was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on Saturday, came to the window in the palace unaided and held his weekly midday appointment as usual. He also urged pilgrims waiting below under cloudy skies to set aside any selfish ambitions and serve God "without compromise". NUN CRIES AS LEO MAKES APPEARANCE Leo has been diagnosed with [USN:L8N46006S TEXT:"lung adenocarcinoma"], the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis, for the youngest pope in decades, who was elected only in May 2025, caused shock. His doctors discharged him on Saturday after blood tests and chest imaging that day showed him well enough to return home. They said he was able to perform normal daily activities independently. Crowds in St. Peter's Square, numbering about 15,000 according to the Vatican, shouted and clapped loudly as Leo first appeared at the window on Sunday. One Catholic nun knelt and cried, holding her hand over her face. A few steps away, a group of other nuns held aloft a sign reading, "Best wishes, Holy Father. We love you and we are praying for you". POPE'S CALENDAR IN FLUX Leo usually keeps a busy schedule, but the Vatican has cancelled his other public events until at least Wednesday, when he is due to hold a weekly general audience in St. Peter's Square. It has not said whether he will hold that audience. The pope is also planning to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader [USN:L8N45D0VL TEXT:"in decades"]. Dr. Stefano Margaritora, the pope's lead surgeon, said on Saturday that Leo could be fully recovered in time for that trip. Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's secretary of state, has however expressed scepticism. He told journalists on Friday the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule going forward "according to the condition of his health".

item.title: Roy Cooper's North Carolina playbook is working. Can other Democrats copy it?
item.description: North Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in nearly 20 years, but former Governor Roy Cooper, who hasn't lost an election in four decades, has built a double-digit lead over Republican Michael Whatley.
item.dc:creator: Yasmeen Abutaleb
item.content:encoded: North Carolina hasn’t elected a Democrat to the US Senate in nearly 20 years, but former Governor Roy Cooper has built a double-digit lead over Republican Michael Whatley by relentlessly focusing on affordability and a blunt promise to “make stuff cost less.” At campaign stops, Cooper, 69, points to his six-year fight to expand Medicaid through a Republican-controlled legislature as evidence he can work across party lines, while attacking Trump-backed healthcare cuts that he says are hitting North Carolinians hard. “People should not have to make a choice between going to a doctor and putting food on the table,” Cooper said at a September 26 rally in Raleigh, North Carolina. “This 'Big Beautiful Bill' that gave tax cuts to billionaires has now driven healthcare premiums up more than double for people.” The White House says the bill cuts taxes, protects Medicaid for eligible Americans and curbs fraud and abuse. Cooper's message appears to be working: His lead stood at 14 points in an October SurveyUSA poll. The top super PAC for Senate Republicans has paused TV advertising in North Carolina less than three weeks before the election and begun shifting campaign dollars to defend seats in states that include Iowa and Kansas. President Donald Trump will rally in the state on Tuesday for Whatley, a former Republican National Committee chair who has never held elected office. The question for Democrats is whether Cooper's playbook can help them win Republican and independent voters elsewhere, or whether his success is unique to a popular former governor who has never lost an election in four decades of public service. While some Democrats in heavily Democratic states have embraced Medicare for All, which would provide government-run health insurance for all Americans, Cooper has focused on expanding existing coverage and lowering costs. He points to his fight to expand Medicaid, the government health insurance program for low-income Americans, and campaigns on prescription drug and insurance costs. 'OUR STAR ATHLETE AND NO ONE'S PAYING ANY ATTENTION' “It’s like he’s our star athlete and no one’s paying any attention,” said Neera Tanden, president of the Center for American Progress, a Democratic-aligned think tank, and former White House adviser to President Joe Biden. “The strength of Roy Cooper’s campaign is that he’s able to attract Democrats and independents, but also even some Republicans because he’s focused on cost, but he also has a record.” Paul Shumaker, a longtime Republican strategist in North Carolina, attributes Cooper’s success to the fact he was already well-known and that Whatley failed to distinguish himself from Trump. “Roy Cooper came to the US Senate race with a known brand that has been trusted by a majority of North Carolina voters election after election,” Shumaker said. “Republicans are suffering from a lack of trust on the economy right now and Whatley has failed to reestablish that trust.” Cooper declined an interview request for this story. The Whatley campaign did not respond to a request for comment, but on Sunday he predicted victory during an interview with Fox News. Trump's upcoming visit to North Carolina and an expected rally with Vice President JD Vance will energize Republican voters, Whatley told Fox News' "Sunday Briefing." "Our election is going to come down to turnout and we're in a state that President Trump won three straight times," Whatley said. WINNING OVER INDEPENDENTS North Carolina’s electorate is unusually independent: 40% of registered voters are unaffiliated with either party, compared with 30% each for Republicans and Democrats. Republicans, however, have dominated the state legislature for more than a decade and redrawn districts to strengthen their grip. Like other Republican candidates, Whatley must contend with Trump’s record-low approval rating, which now hovers at 32%, according to an October [USN:L6N45R10Y TEXT:"Reuters/Ipsos poll"]. That poll also showed registered voters preferring Democrats over Republicans nationally by 44% to 37%. Among independents, Democrats led 37% to 21%, with 28% of independent voters still undecided. Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the US Senate, where Democrats must net four seats in the November 3 midterm elections to control the chamber — an already difficult task that makes Cooper's North Carolina race especially important. Cooper's signature bipartisan achievement did not come easily. It took him six years to persuade the Republican-controlled state legislature to pass an expansion of Medicaid under Obamacare in 2023, extending health insurance to more than 700,000 state residents, according to state health department data. After passage, he called it “an unnecessarily long and agonizing journey.” Whit Ayres, a Republican pollster, said several moderate Democratic governors in the South could replicate Cooper’s success, including Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear. “The Roy Coopers of the world are not unique,” Ayres said. “The Republicans nominated someone who’s never been elected to any public office at any level anywhere running against a reasonably moderate, popular governor.” RUNNING AGAINST HEALTHCARE CUTS Many of the state’s Medicaid gains are likely to be undone by Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill,” a sweeping tax and budget bill the Republican-led Congress passed last year that cuts about $1 trillion from Medicaid, the largest cut in the program’s history, according to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office. Cooper has used Trump’s signature domestic legislative achievement to paint the president and Republicans as depriving North Carolinians of healthcare in order to give billionaires more tax cuts. He has also focused on congressional Republicans’ decision to curtail COVID-era Obamacare subsidies last year, causing healthcare premiums on the individual health insurance marketplace to spike and more than 200,000 state residents to drop their coverage, according to health policy research firm KFF. “Roy Cooper has always polled over Republicans,” said Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party. “This will be the average election for Roy Cooper.”

item.title: Microsoft pulls out of UK data center deal with Nscale, Telegraph reports
item.description: Microsoft has pulled out of a data center deal with British cloud provider Nscale, Britain's Telegraph newspaper reported on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Microsoft (MSFT.O) has pulled out of a data center deal with British cloud provider Nscale, Britain's Telegraph newspaper reported on Sunday. The US tech giant, one of Nscale's two largest customers, recently terminated its agreement for the data center in Loughton, Essex, according to the report. The newspaper did not specify why Microsoft withdrew from the project. Microsoft declined a Reuters request for comment. The Telegraph report said Nscale had faced repeated delays with the project. National power grid officials, it reported, had told Nscale they did not expect a power supply for the data center until the 2030s. "Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," an Nscale spokesperson told Reuters. "We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK." Nscale filed for an [USN:L4N45A197 TEXT:"initial public offering"] in the US last month, with Microsoft and Anthropic expected to be its major customers, according to its prospectus. Nscale [USN:L4N45A1JP TEXT:"provides"] infrastructure, including compute, power and data centers, as well as software for training and running AI models. The Nvidia-backed (NVDA.O) AI group, which competes against CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , Nebius (NBIS.O) , Crusoe and Lambda, has grown rapidly since its launch, scaling from $100 million to more than $103 billion in total contracted value in just two-and-a-half years.

item.title: Macron urges calm as France counts cost of worst unrest in years
item.description: The French president appealed for calm a day after France suffered one of its worst days of unrest in years, with thousands arrested and shops looted or damaged after protests over high prices and declining public services.
item.dc:creator: Sybille de La Hamaide, Clotaire Achi, Abdul Saboor
item.content:encoded: President Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Sunday, a day after France suffered one of its worst days of unrest in years, with thousands arrested and shops looted or damaged after protests over high prices and declining public services. Fresh clashes broke out in Paris and Marseille, where riot police intervened to prevent attempts to ransack businesses. Nationwide demonstrations had erupted into riots on Saturday, with a town hall torched, shops pillaged and buildings covered in graffiti as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country. "Looking at these images, we have all asked ourselves: What was going through their minds? How can French people do this to France?" Macron said in a televised address to the nation. "Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it, nothing excuses it. Tonight, we all feel anger and shame." Saturday's unrest laid bare the deep anger at Macron, who leaves office in 2027 after a decade in power that has increasingly become defined by social discontent, a weak economy and ballooning debt. Macron said those protesting peacefully had legitimate grievances and their actions should not be confused with those seeking to wreak havoc. He stopped short of declaring a state of emergency, as demanded by some right-wing politicians, but said the government would act to allow prefects to ban protests if necessary to protect public buildings and local businesses. PARIS PROTESTS 'LIKE A WAR ZONE' The government has blamed the violence on what it said were ultra-left groups, as well as criminals it said had instigated the looting. One protester died on Saturday after suffering a cardiac arrest during [USN:L1N46302B TEXT:"demonstrations"] in Paris. Police made 2,400 arrests across France, while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said. Police again clashed with protesters and fired tear gas at Place de la Republique on Sunday afternoon, and protesters had set fire to piles of bicycles. A Reuters witness said there appeared to be several hundred protesters in the area. A massive clean-up operation took place in cities from Lille in the north to Marseille in the south and from Strasbourg in the east to Bordeaux in the southwest, where a masked mob invaded the residence of the local prefect. "It's like a war zone here!" exclaimed Dutch entrepreneur Tije De Boer, who was visiting Paris with his children and said the unrest forced him to evacuate his hotel at Place de la Republique. More than half a million people joined marches in scores of cities on Saturday, marking the convergence of a month-long [USN:L6N45M1EJ TEXT:"student movement"] with broader social discontent against rising living costs and declining public services. SEVERAL HUNDRED SHOPS DAMAGED While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully across France on Saturday, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers. Far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, frontrunner going into next year's presidential campaign, also called for calm, saying France must not become accustomed to images of the country being battered, abused and ransacked. "Violence is not an opinion. Destruction is not a form of expression. And chaos cannot serve as a project for France," she said in a video address. Hard-left France Unbowed presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon said Macron needed to answer the demands of protesting high-school students. In [USN:L1N46402C TEXT:"Limoges"], famed for its porcelain, the collapse of the town hall's clock tower in a fiery blaze revived memories of the 2019 fire that devastated Paris' Notre Dame cathedral. Mayor Guillaume Guerin said not enough officers from the national police had been deployed to his city. "There was a clear, premeditated intention to burn down the town hall, and the people inside feared for their lives," Guerin told Reuters on Sunday. He threatened to resign if the city did not receive the funds needed to repair the town hall. Economy Minister Roland Lescure pledged support on Sunday for business owners who suffered losses. "Those who break things will pay, repair the damage and be held accountable for their intention to sow chaos," Lescure said in a statement. French retailer Carrefour's (CARR.PA) CEO Alexandre Bompard told French broadcaster BFMTV that 50 of the company's shops had been damaged, including 20 that were looted, with losses from the damage running into the tens of millions of euros.

item.title: Iran's parliament approves Mehrdad Akhlaqi as minister of defence
item.description: Iran's parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defence minister on Sunday, ending months of interim leadership at the ministry and placing a former defence sector veteran in charge of the country's defence production and procurement apparatus.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Iran's parliament approved Mehrdad Akhlaqi Ketabchi as defence minister on Sunday, ending months of interim leadership at the ministry and placing a former defence sector veteran in charge of the country's defence production and procurement apparatus. Akhlaqi replaces Majid Ebn al-Reza, who took over in an interim capacity after then Defence Minister Aziz Nasirzadeh was killed by US-Israeli strikes in February. Akhlaqi has spent decades in Iran's defence industry and has held senior roles in its aerospace and missile sectors. He is subject to US and EU sanctions over his work in Iran's defence sector. In a programme presented to lawmakers, Akhlaqi pledged to rebuild the country's military-industrial infrastructure, accelerate the development of defence technologies and expand cooperation with private-sector companies. "If the American enemy makes another miscalculation, the response of the valiant Iranian people and the fighters of Islam will be surprising and extensive," he said, adding that Tehran had taken necessary measures to counter the potential use by the US of its "mother of all bombs" against Iran. CNN reported this week that the [USN:FWN46108H TEXT:"US has developed"] strike plans that could include using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, also known as the "mother of all bombs", against Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites if President Donald Trump orders renewed combat operations. The weapon is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the US arsenal. "The US President should focus on ensuring his forces are withdrawn safely from our region. If he drops a single bomb, he will have to see how many of his troops end up being carried out of the region in a horizontal position," Akhlaqi said.

item.title: China's solar panel exports extend slump in September
item.description: China's solar power equipment exports fell 6.4% in September from the same month last year, customs data showed on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: China's solar power equipment exports fell 6.4% in September from the same month last year, customs data showed on Sunday. China, the world's largest solar manufacturer, exported 1.21 million metric tons of solar cells and panels in September. That was down from September a year earlier but up from 840,000 tons in August. In the year through September, China exported 9.37 million tons of the equipment, down 9.5%. September solar exports were valued at $3.34 billion, up 19.4%. On a per-unit basis, China shipped 11.3% more cells and panels, or 1.44 billion.

item.title: China proposes export controls on solar-manufacturing technologies
item.description: China has proposed export controls on 12 technologies used to make solar equipment, citing national security concerns, as part of a broader revision that also covers AI and biotechnology.
item.dc:creator: Colleen Howe
item.content:encoded: China has proposed export controls on 12 technologies used to make solar equipment, citing national security concerns, as part of a [USN:P8N44A04L TEXT:"broader revision"] that also covers AI and biotechnology. The ministry of commerce proposed adding the photovoltaic technologies to China's export-control list, it said in a statement on Friday, adding that greater oversight is needed because solar technologies are increasingly being used in sensitive areas like aerospace and national defense. Chinese officials held [USN:L1N40Y0TZ TEXT:"initial talks"] with manufacturers about potential curbs on advanced solar-panel manufacturing technologies, Reuters reported in April, a move that could threaten plans by US firms such as Tesla (TSLA.O) to [USN:L6N4080PX TEXT:"expand production"] in the US. Beijing has also curbed exports of solar-manufacturing technology to [USN:L4N43A1F4 TEXT:"India,"] Reuters has reported. Analysts say China is seeking to preserve its dominance as India tries to build up domestic manufacturing and shake off reliance on China. Export restrictions aim to "guard against the risks of technologies from running out of control or being improperly disseminated, while safeguarding normal international exchanges and cooperation in science and technology," the ministry said. Exporters must now register certain overseas technology transfers until the export-control catalogue is formally updated. Public consultation on the proposal will close on November 15. China would ban technologies including those used to make some thin wafers, perovskite and tandem solar cells, as well as large-scale fluidized-bed polysilicon production technologies. Perovskite is an emerging technology that offers the potential of increased conversion efficiency. Tandem cells combine perovskite and silicon layers to capture more of the sunlight spectrum. Fluidized-bed technology for producing polysilicon — a key building block for solar panels — is less expensive and more energy-efficient than the dominant Siemens process. China would also restrict, but not prohibit, exports of advanced solar cell manufacturing technologies, including TOPCon, HJT and XBC.

item.title: Lithuanians forced to take shelter after suspected drone enters airspace
item.description: Ukraine's foreign ministry said the incident may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting its drones off course.
item.dc:creator: Andrius Sytas
item.content:encoded: A suspected drone exploded over Lithuania after triggering an alert that forced residents in northern and central areas to seek shelter for an hour on Sunday morning, the president and other defence officials said. Ukraine 's Foreign Ministry [USN:L8N46404Q TEXT:"said"] later it regretted the incident in Lithuania's airspace, adding that it may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones off course. The object flew into Lithuania's airspace from Poland, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told reporters, after proposing a joint investigation to his Polish counterpart. "Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU," Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said on X. "What appears to be a drone exploded over the northern part of the country, posing a danger to the civilian population," he added. NATO SCRAMBLES FIGHTERS Poland's military said it was also [USN:FWN4630JH TEXT:"verifying a possible violation of its airspace"] by an unidentified object. A Polish Defence Ministry spokesperson later said radar systems did not confirm the object crossing the border into Lithuania, but added that Polish authorities were remaining in contact with Lithuanian officials. During the "red" alert, NATO fighter jets were scrambled to the area, and Kaunas airport, near Lithuania's second-largest city, was temporarily closed, the Lithuanian government's crisis management centre said. The NATO aircraft were unable to visually identify the object due to cloudy weather and did not attempt to shoot it down, the centre said. Lithuanian army personnel were investigating possible drone debris near Juodzionys village in northern Lithuania, after the object disappeared from radar, possibly after exploding, the centre said. Some of the debris struck a civilian vehicle, Kaunas said. "We can confirm that two Italian Eurofighter jets were scrambled earlier today in response to a drone over Lithuanian airspace," a NATO official said. "The aircraft were operating under NATO command. An investigation is ongoing, and NATO remains in close contact with the Lithuanian authorities," the official said, adding that the alliance was ready and able to react to any potential threat. Northern neighbour Latvia briefly issued a "yellow" air warning in some regions bordering Lithuania, citing a "possible threat", its army said. Ukrainian drones have repeatedly [USN:L8N41X1AC TEXT:"entered NATO airspace"] in the Baltic region in recent months. Kyiv has said they were steered off course by Russian signal jamming. This has stoked concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling over NATO's borders.

item.title: Vietnam signs free-trade pact with European countries including Norway, Switzerland
item.description: Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein have signed a free-trade agreement with Vietnam, the governments of Norway and Vietnam announced on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein have signed a free-trade agreement with Vietnam, the governments of Norway and Vietnam announced on Sunday. Vietnam's trade ministry said it signed the deal in Hanoi with the European Free Trade Association members. Around half of Norway's exports to Vietnam will be tariff-free when the agreement enters into force, with more than 98% to be tariff-free within seven years, the Norwegian government said in a statement. Long-stalled free-trade talks were [USN:L6N4600OA TEXT:"relaunched last year"] amid global tensions over US tariffs. [USN:L8N4340QC TEXT:"Negotiations concluded"] in July. Vietnam's trade ministry said the Southeast Asian country mainly exports seafood, footwear, textiles, machinery and equipment, electronics and components to the EFTA market and imports industrial machinery and equipment, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and raw materials for production. Bilateral trade between Vietnam and EFTA member countries has averaged $2 billion annually, the ministry said.

item.title: Rubio arrives in Central Asia while other US officials hit foreign policy hot spots
item.description: While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges.
item.dc:creator: Gram Slattery, Simon Lewis
item.content:encoded: While the Iran war smolders, Saudi Arabia fights the Houthis and a new rift opens in US-Ukraine relations, Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled on Sunday to Uzbekistan, a nation far removed from the biggest US foreign policy challenges. The top US diplomat landed in Samarkand on Sunday night to meet with top officials from the C5+1, a grouping that brings together the United States and the Muslim-majority post-Soviet states of Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan and Turkmenistan. US officials have portrayed resource-rich Central Asia — the region between China, Russia and Iran — as worthy of more attention than it received from US President Donald Trump's predecessors. Trump hosted C5 leaders at the White House last November, when Kazakhstan agreed to join the Abraham Accords, a series of agreements under which Muslim-majority countries have normalized or deepened relations with Israel. Separately, Trump met with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev at the United Nations General Assembly in September of last year. Regional politics aside, the trip fits an emerging pattern in which Rubio often visits regions not at the center of the news cycle, while leaving some more fraught foreign policy portfolios to other Trump aides, including special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and Vice President JD Vance. Rubio has not visited Kyiv or Moscow since becoming secretary of state and was not present for talks between US and Ukrainian officials in Florida earlier this month, when US officials pressed Ukraine to stop hitting Russian refineries. Vance, not Rubio, represented the US in Pakistan during peace talks with Iran in April. Rubio's previous foreign trip, in early October, took him to Greece, Portugal and Iceland. Trump administration officials have typically rejected any suggestion that cabinet-level officials should focus their travels on geopolitical capitals and hot spots. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, for instance, said on X last week that the idea only certain destinations were worthy of visits from secretaries of state "perfectly encapsulates the decadence and degeneracy of the contemporary US foreign policy establishment." Speaking to reporters before leaving Washington on Saturday, Rubio said the timing of the Uzbekistan trip was dictated in part by the availability of the various delegations. He also said that foreign trips were too often designed to resolve immediate issues rather than build long-term relationships. "I mean, one of the things that suffers is the strategic business," Rubio told reporters. "You're always visiting someplace where there's a crisis or there's a problem or ... you're going because there's a conference." US-RUSSIA RELATIONS LOOM The delegation that greeted Rubio upon his arrival in Samarkand included Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov, whom Rubio embraced warmly. Two women in traditional Uzbek attire presented Rubio and his wife with bouquets. One Central Asian diplomat, speaking on the condition of anonymity, said officials in the region were wondering to what extent the US would continue targeting Russian sanctions evasion. All C5 states, while drawing closer to the US, have deep historical ties with Moscow, and the region has facilitated Russian imports and exports that violate US and European Union sanctions, Western officials say. In the past, the US has pushed regional states to clamp down on those illicit flows. But Trump struck a deal with Moscow this month to [USN:L1N45Y0GJ TEXT:"import Russian diesel"], aimed at lowering domestic fuel prices before congressional midterm elections. On Friday, Trump [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"waived"] all provisions of legislation that would have allowed him to slap massive tariffs on some nations that buy significant amounts of Russian crude oil or otherwise help Moscow evade sanctions. Among the nations that could have been affected, experts have said, are India and Kazakhstan. India, which Rubio will visit after Uzbekistan, remains the world's No. 2 Russian crude importer after China, despite Trump saying in February that India had agreed to stop buying oil from Russia. Additional questions hang over a potential trade deal with India and an expansion of the Abraham Accords in Central Asia. A US official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, described the trade deal on Friday as "pretty much done," raising the possibility that an agreement could be announced during the Rubio trip. Separately, the US [USN:L1N3TQ0WH TEXT:"has talked to"] additional Central Asian nations about joining the Abraham Accords, Reuters reported last year, conversations that potentially could continue in Samarkand. More than 200 business executives are accompanying Rubio to Uzbekistan, the State Department said. The Central Asian diplomat said the Trump administration has focused its commercial efforts on expanding access to the area's rare earth mineral resources. After Uzbekistan, Rubio will visit the Indian cities of Mumbai and Jamnagar to meet with business leaders, including Reliance Industries (RELI.NS) Chairman Mukesh Ambani, who earned the Trump administration's favor earlier in the year by backing a new refinery in Texas. Rubio most recently visited India five months ago. The trip is due to wrap up on Thursday.

item.title: Rubio says Trump to take up to 60 days to weigh Russia sanctions
item.description: Ukraine's Zelenskiy says sanctions waiver will prolong war with Russia.
item.dc:creator: Nandita Bose, Gram Slattery
item.content:encoded: The day after waiving sanctions and tariffs related to Russian exports, US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he has yet to announce a final decision on the matter, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials want more time to evaluate the situation. Rubio said on Saturday that the president will use up to 60 days to assess the economic impact of Russia-related sanctions and tariffs that he waived a day earlier. "A lot of you don't know what my decision is yet, but we'll figure it out, and you'll figure it out," Trump told reporters at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida. In a Truth Social post on Sunday, Trump wrote that his decision-making was aimed at avoiding anything "that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table." Trump signed an executive order on Friday waiving key sanctions and tariffs under the law known as the Graham Act, which he signed last month at the urging of lawmakers who want to pressure Moscow over its war in Ukraine. The measures, including tariffs on Russian goods and penalties on countries buying Russian oil and gas, were due to take effect next week. Friday's order did not specify how long the waiver would last, but Rubio said Trump opted for a 60-day review. "I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy," Rubio told reporters before boarding a plane for a trip to Uzbekistan. Friday's executive order [USN:L1N463009 TEXT:"drew criticism"] from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, who warned it would embolden Russian President Vladimir Putin and prolong the war. DIESEL SUPPLIES Rubio on Saturday also defended a separate US agreement with Russia to increase diesel supplies to global markets, aimed at easing fuel prices that have climbed amid the war with Iran and disruptions to energy supplies. "That diesel is going to be sold one way or the other," Rubio said. "The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get." Under the agreement, Trump said Russia initially would supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the United States, followed by shipments in November and beyond. The diesel agreement is "a carrot to try to end the war, not an economic lifeline" to Russia, US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said during a Sunday interview on ABC's "This Week." But "the only way they can get additional diesel to export is if they turn down the conflict with Ukraine," Wright told CNN's "State of the Union" program on Sunday. “If Russia can bring additional diesel to the market and export it, it would benefit American consumers,” he told CNN. “He's putting pressure that would both benefit American consumers and be a step forward for peace in the Russia-Ukraine war.” Rubio said the diesel deal and sanctions waiver reflected the challenge of managing conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine that have disrupted global energy supplies. "These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other," he said.

item.title: Saudi-led coalition says helicopter crash in Najran kills two crew members
item.description: A reconnaissance AH-6i helicopter crashed in the Najran region of Saudi Arabia, killing its two crew members, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on Sunday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: A reconnaissance AH-6i helicopter crashed in the Najran region of Saudi Arabia, killing its two crew members, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a statement on Sunday. The helicopter crashed due to a technical malfunction in an area under the jurisdiction of the Saudi National Guard Ministry, the statement added. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis released footage later on Sunday of what they said was a Saudi AH-6i helicopter being shot down by a missile while carrying out what they described as hostile activities near Najran. The footage did not clearly show the incident, and Reuters could not immediately verify the Houthis' claim. There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities. On Saturday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X that the group had shot down a Saudi Apache helicopter near Najran. It was not clear if that referred to the same incident. Al-Maliki commented on Saree's post on Sunday with a photo of several Apaches lined up, saying: "You claim to have shot it down, but it will enter the battlefield soon." Separately, the Saudi civil defence said on Sunday that six people were injured after a projectile it said was fired by Houthis fell on a residential area in Najran. Najran has been hit by attacks from the Houthis in recent weeks as fighting between the coalition and the Yemen-based group escalated, with the [USN:L1N4620VJ TEXT:"Yemen conflict"] becoming another front in the US-led war with Iran .

item.title: Woodside natural gas project unit paused after Greenpeace protest off Western Australia
item.description: Woodside said operations remained paused on Sunday at a floating production unit, part of its $12.5 billion Scarborough natural gas project off the coast of Western Australia, due to a Greenpeace protest at the platform.
item.dc:creator: Samuel Mckeith
item.content:encoded: Woodside (WDS.AX) said operations remained paused on Sunday at a floating production unit, part of its $12.5 billion Scarborough natural gas project off the coast of Western Australia, due to a Greenpeace protest at the platform. Two activists from the environmental advocacy group slept overnight on the semi-submersible unit, located around 375 km (233 miles) off the state's northwest coast, in the [USN:L4N46300J TEXT:"protest"] that started on Saturday, Greenpeace said. "Temporary hanging tents" were set up on the unit and the activists would "occupy the platform for as long as possible," Greenpeace said. The group is concerned about the potential impact of Woodside's proposed Browse project on Scott Reef, a remote coral system and foraging area for the endangered pygmy blue whale. Woodside has said it expects no physical contact with the reef above the 75-metre (246-foot) water depth. A Woodside spokesperson said "operations at the Scarborough FPU remain safely paused" on Sunday, a day after temporarily halting pre-commissioning activities as a result of the "unauthorised access". Four activists on Saturday scaled the 70,000 metric ton unit, part of the 98% completed Scarborough project, and displayed banners with the message "Stop Woodside’s Dirty Gas. Save Scott Reef", according to Greenpeace. Australian Border Force on Sunday said it had no update on the incident. It previously said it was working with federal and state agencies on a response.

item.title: US wants Israel to 'crack down' on settler violence in West Bank, Rubio says
item.description: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Marco Rubio said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The United States wants Israel to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers in the West Bank, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday. "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing," Rubio said. "We've asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack down on that stuff." His comments to reporters came after the widespread dissemination of video showing multiple individuals attacking Heidi Levine, an American photojournalist with the Washington Post. Levine was one of at least two people injured in the Friday incident, which took place as Israeli settlers [USN:L6N46304S TEXT:"attacked"] Palestinian civilians. European diplomats and a French mayor also were attacked in the occupied West Bank, Belgium's foreign minister said. The US State Department, Rubio said, has inquired about the event that included Levine's attack. Rubio, who spoke to reporters before boarding a flight to Uzbekistan, said he expects to hear back from the US Embassy in Jerusalem by Sunday. Israeli settlers in the West Bank have been involved in at least 170 attacks on Palestinians since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, according to Yesh Din, an Israeli settlements monitoring group.

item.description: The cases are the first known infections passed on inside Kenya, where the first patient arrived from Congo on Oct 3.

Kenya confirmed four new cases of the Ebola Bundibugyo virus on Saturday (Oct 17), including three health workers who treated the country's first patient, bringing the total number of confirmed cases to seven, the health ministry said. The other new case is a male relative of the index patient, who died. The relative had been in quarantine since Oct 6, the ministry said in a statement. The cases are the first known infections passed on inside Kenya, where the first patient arrived from Congo on Oct 3. But the ministry says it has traced and quarantined nearly all of his contacts and there is no evidence that the virus is spreading in the community . The three health workers, two men and a woman aged 29, 35 and 32 respectively, managed the index case on Oct 3 and 4 and had been in quarantine since Oct 9, it said. All four new patients were already in quarantine when they developed symptoms and were diagnosed.

The second and third patients confirmed earlier are stable and responding well to supportive treatment, the ministry said. It said 128 of 130 listed contacts, or 98.5 percent, had been traced and placed in quarantine, higher than the 85 percent global benchmark it said was needed to break the chain of transmission. Kenya's cases are linked to the Ebola epidemic in Congo, the second-largest outbreak ever recorded, with more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,000 deaths.

Related:

Tan Kiat How on low risk of Ebola cross-border transmission to Singapore

WHO says Congo Ebola outbreak can still be brought under control within three months

Commentary: This Ebola outbreak should never have caught the world off guard

There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola. The first Kenyan case was a man who had been ill in Congo for about a month before travelling by road to Uganda and flying to Nairobi on Oct 3. He died on Oct 5. His arrival has raised concerns about screening at the Congo-Uganda border, which has been closed since May, and at Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. Efforts to trace the remaining two contacts were ongoing, the ministry said. "The risk to the general public remains low as there is no evidence of community transmission," it said, adding that there were no restrictions on travel, trade or public gatherings.

Source: Reuters/fs

item.title: Egypt's Sisi says his presidency will end in 2030, outlines plan to prepare future leaders
item.description: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months before then.
item.dc:creator: Enas Alashray
item.content:encoded: Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi said on Saturday that his term would end in 2030 and outlined a plan for the country's main military academy to train potential future leaders for 30 months before then. The proposal gives the Egyptian Military Academy a central role in preparing future leaders, underscoring the armed forces' influence beyond national defence. Under Sisi, a former general, the military has expanded its presence in the economy and civilian affairs. Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the academy, Sisi said a committee overseen by the speaker of parliament and including intellectuals, politicians and the ministers of higher education and justice, would develop criteria for selecting candidates and draft legislation for the training programme. Reiterating that Egypt's constitution would not be amended, he said the end of his presidential term in 2030 was "a matter that has been completely settled and will not be discussed". He said the programme would allow Egyptians to "elect and choose from among" its graduates, but gave no details on how they would be put forward for elected or appointed posts. "I will not leave the Egyptian state except when it is replete with sons and daughters capable of assuming responsibility," Sisi said. The programme would target PhD holders from reputable Egyptian and foreign universities, who would spend 30 months at the academy learning about the state, its resources and how to preserve them, Sisi said. He said graduates would be prepared for leadership roles ranging from the presidency to ministries, governorates and parliament. [USN:L5N3GA3X9 TEXT:"Sisi"], 71, is serving a six-year term after being reelected in December 2023. Constitutional amendments approved in a 2019 referendum extended presidential terms from four to six years and allowed him to seek a third term, clearing the way for him to remain in office until 2030. The latest in a line of Egyptian rulers drawn from the military, he became president in 2014, a year after toppling Mohamed Morsi of the Muslim Brotherhood — Egypt's first democratically elected leader — following mass protests. He proceeded to crush the Brotherhood, the Middle East's oldest Islamist organisation, and maintain a grip on power.

item.title: Indian state food safety authority names Reliance, Blinkit executives in expired food probe
item.description: India's food safety authority has named officials of Reliance retail and consumer units and of Eternal’s Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food products that have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Arpan Chaturvedi
item.content:encoded: India's food safety authority has named officials of Reliance retail and consumer units and of Eternal’s Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food products that have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters. The Food and Drug Administration of Maharashtra state, home to Mumbai, has led a [USN:L4N44Z0MR TEXT:"crackdown"] on food safety under its chief Tukaram Mundhe, 51, including shutting down some of Mumbai’s most popular eateries as well as outlets of Domino’s and Pizza Hut for poor hygiene. The state agency has also suspended the permit of a McDonald’s outlet. The latest case, which has led to a police complaint by the food safety authority, involves large retail and quick-commerce companies, which sell products to millions of households in the world’s most populous country. Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, according to the documents reviewed by Reuters, said its officials visited some warehouses of Reliance Retail, Reliance Consumer and Zomato Hyperpure, and that company officials could not provide verifiable proof that disposal of expired food was actually carried out by their contractors. "The disposal agencies ... do not destroy the stock," the case document alleged. In the case of a Zomato Hyperpure warehouse, a company representative named a contractor as its disposal agency which FDA officials could not trace, according to the documents. Reliance and Blinkit did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. "Any attempt to divert expired, damaged or consumer-rejected food products meant for destruction back into the market is a serious matter that demands strict scrutiny and accountability," Maharashtra's FDA chief Tukaram Mundhe told Reuters. "No company, brand, business or individual is above the law when it comes to food safety." INDIA'S INTENSIFYING CRACKDOWN Reliance Retail and Reliance Consumer are part of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s business group. Zomato’s Hyperpure is a unit of Eternal that also runs food delivery service Zomato and quick commerce business Blinkit. The FDA probe said it found a pattern where large retail and quick commerce distribution warehouses handed over expired and customer-rejected packages of food to contractors who passed the food to unlicensed sorting yards. These sorting yards then separated out saleable-looking packets, which eventually reached other retailers and the consumer market, according to case documents from the probe. "The chain thus runs from company warehouse to disposal agency, unlicensed yard, broker, retailer and consumer." The Maharashtra FDA on Thursday suspended the licences of five establishments in the state — three Reliance and two Eternal entities, the case documents said. Enforcement of food safety laws has traditionally been weak in India and the recent round of extensive crackdowns has garnered large-scale public support. In August, Indian authorities [USN:L4N44S18T TEXT:"raided"] an illegal operation in Mumbai that faked expiry dates and nutritional information on original food products manufactured by PepsiCo (PEP.O) , Nestle (NESN.S) , Coca-Cola (KO.N) and Unilever, so they could be exported to other countries. (This story has been corrected to say 'Reliance retail and consumer units,' not 'Reliance Group entities,' in paragraph 1.)

item.title: AI rapidly improving, could vastly boost US GDP, Anthropic's Clark tells policymakers
item.description: Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030.
item.dc:creator: David Lawder
item.content:encoded: Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal models forecasting that under certain conditions it could increase US economic output by almost 50% by 2030. Clark, speaking at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said that international cooperation was needed to erect "unusual and serious rules" for the transformative technology, and there was a shrinking window for policymakers to act. Clark said that the estimated potential US GDP of $44 trillion, which compares to the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish, I know." But he added that AI was vastly increasing scientific discovery. He said the forecast assumed "the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion". Clark's remarks come as the company prepares for an [USN:L6N4611F6 TEXT:"initial public offering"] expected in November that could value the firm at up to $2 trillion. HUMANS IN CONTROL, FOR NOW Clark issued a wake-up call to policymakers about the speed of AI development, saying there was growing evidence of a "singularity" where AI development outpaces human control. "We should expect that in the coming years, the whole pace of progress of not just AI but science as a whole will speed up, and this will feel confusing and disorienting, and will bring with it great wealth and potentially great peril," he said in a lecture to hundreds of government and finance officials. AI was a major topic at the IMF and World Bank meetings, as both a [USN:L1N45Z01U TEXT:"source of growth"] offsetting high energy prices and a potential threat to stability if it falls short of its promise as a productivity game-changer and stock valuations crash. Officials also expressed worries about AI destroying certain jobs and leaving some countries behind. But Clark, a former journalist who serves as Anthropic's "head of public benefit," painted a picture of a rosy future where AI was a force multiplier for scientific discovery, solving mathematical, engineering and biological problems, including new drug discovery, as human researchers are supplemented by hundreds or thousands of AI assistants. More countries can participate in the AI revolution by helping to build the data center computing capacity needed to power AI, he said. STRICTEST CONTROLS ON BIOLOGICAL RESEARCH Clark cautioned that global leaders need to understand how powerful AI will become and make urgent choices about how to regulate the technology. "Being able to use AI for science opens us up to the misuses of science as well, biological and cyber weapons and things we cannot yet imagine, and we have many choices to make," he said. Biological research, where AI has already created new viruses, is an area "where we want the strictest human oversight and transparency to maintain safety." Despite some recent high-profile incidents where [USN:L4N45N1OZ TEXT:"rogue AI systems"] have escaped testing environments and hacked websites and databases, he said AI was still under human control. But the window to impose safeguards was shrinking as AI became more capable and was now "a small number of years." Clark also acknowledged that AI was causing job losses in some fields with "high AI exposure" such as call centers and customer service personnel. But for other fields, such as scientific research, he said AI was enhancing employment and a major unknown was its potential to create jobs in completely new industries.

item.title: ソフトバンクＧ、米警備大手アライド買収検討＝関係筋
item.description:
Milana Vinn
[１６日 ロイター] - ソフトバンクグループが米警備サービス大手アライド・ユニバーサルの...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
ソフトバンクＧ、米警備大手アライド買収検討＝関係筋 10/17 15:08 配信

ソフトバンクグループのロゴ。９月東京で撮影。REUTERS/Manami Yamada

Milana Vinn

[１６日 ロイター] - ソフトバンクグループが米警備サービス大手アライド・ユニバーサルの買収を検討している。関係者が１６日明らかにした。買収案では、アライドの評価額が約１８０億ドルになる可能性がある。

アライドは企業や各種施設、大規模イベントに警備員を派遣する事業を手がける。データセンター分野でも事業を拡大しており、施設の開発と運営の両面を支援している。

ソフトバンクはアライドの買収が実現すれば、特定の警備業務で人員の一部をいずれロボットに置き換えることを目指す。ただ人型ロボットの警備業務への導入には長い時間がかかるとみられる。

買収検討は初期段階にあり、買収額を含め、最終決定には至っていないという。

item.title: BOJ may need to tighten faster if inflation beats forecast, IMF says
item.description: The Bank of Japan is "doing the right thing" by normalising monetary policy and may need to raise interest rates faster if inflation rises more than expected, a senior International Monetary Fund official told Reuters.
item.dc:creator: Leika Kihara
item.content:encoded: The Bank of Japan is "doing the right thing" by normalising monetary policy and may need to raise interest rates faster if inflation rises more than expected, a senior International Monetary Fund official told Reuters. Japan must also clarify how it plans to fund its big spending plans and lay out a medium-term fiscal framework to ease market concerns about fiscal risks, said Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department. "I would say that they are doing the right thing at this point," Srinivasan said on the BOJ's efforts to lift its policy rate towards levels deemed neutral to the economy. "If inflation rises faster than expected, you have to start tightening faster because you don't want inflation expectations to get un-anchored. It's data dependent," he said in an interview on Friday. The remarks came ahead of the BOJ's key policy meeting later this month, when it [USN:L4N45S011 TEXT:"could keep rates steady"] but drop hawkish hints that would reinforce dominant market expectations of a December hike. Inflationary pressures from the Middle East conflict and brisk AI-demand were among key themes discussed by policymakers gathering for this week's annual IMF meetings in Bangkok. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda, who attended the IMF meetings, said on [USN:L1N4620G5 TEXT:"Friday"] the central bank will focus on anchoring underlying inflation around its 2% target and won't tolerate any overshoot, stressing anew its resolve to continue raising interest rates. For Japan, a weak yen adds to factors pushing up inflation by boosting the cost of raw material imports. Such mounting price pressures prodded the BOJ to raise rates to a 31-year high of 1.25% in [USN:L1N459138 TEXT:"September"], following a hike in June. Many analysts expect another rate increase by year-end. Japan also conducted a rare, coordinated intervention with the US on [USN:L1N43Z05E TEXT:"July 31"] to prevent the currency's slide to near 40-year lows from destabilising financial markets. In staff analysis included in its report on Asia's economy, the IMF said a big portion of yen moves since mid-2025 had little to do with fundamental factors such as yield differentials, and instead co-moved with speculative positions in yen futures. "Japan has a deep foreign exchange market, so as a first line of defense, they have allowed the exchange rate to move," Srinivasan said. "Bottom line, I would say that the Japanese authorities are fully committed to a freely floating exchange rate. I've had many discussions with them. So I don't doubt that at all," he said when asked if the recent yen intervention was justified. FISCAL FRAMEWORK NEEDED Rising global bond yields have also drawn attention at this week's IMF meetings as debt in advanced economies, including Japan, expanded after years of heavy spending. Markets worry that Japan may add to its already huge debt pile with the administration's big spending plans and a two-year cut to the consumption tax from April next year. Srinivasan said Japan has in fact seen fiscal consolidation proceed more than any other G7 country since the pandemic due in part to rising tax revenues. "Markets are concerned about the fiscal risks because of the uncertainty" on how Japan would pay for the fresh spending and tax-cut plans, he said. "Japan also would benefit from having a medium-term fiscal framework."

item.title: Bangladesh is battling measles. It's a 'real warning' to other nations
item.description: Bangladesh's vaccination program was a success story until it faltered because of political turmoil. Its unvaccinated children are paying the price.
item.dc:creator: Ruma Paul, Jennifer Rigby, Sam Jahan, Zia Chowdhury
item.content:encoded: The parents of Labiba Akter have kept a blue dress once worn by their nine-month-old daughter, who died of measles in June, as a keepsake. They were not told she was eligible for a vaccination before she contracted the disease. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain Bangladesh is battling to contain the world’s worst measles outbreak , a crisis exacerbated by weak data, inadequate outreach and vaccination gaps that experts say offers a warning to other nations about the deadly risk of falling immunisation rates. Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination programme faltered in 2025, reported 202,000 suspected measles cases – 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed – since the start of the outbreak in mid-March to October 9, the World Health Organization said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year. So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94% of reported deaths among children under five years old, the WHO said. Bangladesh's experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95%, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years but in 2025 coverage dropped. A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents. "This is a real warning to every country," said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University. Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations was easier, cheaper and safer than responding to an emergency, he said. "The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died," he said. Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article. Amin Mia and Sajina Begum pose with their four-year-old daughter who survived measles. Below, Sajina Begum shows a photo of her husband, daughter and two-year-old son, Arman Hossain, who died of the disease in July. Neither child received a vaccination. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain ‘THEY CAME ONLY AFTER I BURIED MY SON’ In the northeast Sylhet region, one of the worst-hit areas in the nation of 178 million people, two-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family's three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated four-year-old sister survived. His father Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. "They came only after I buried my son," he said. Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer nations because of factors such as malnutrition. This is a real warning to every country. Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June aged nine months. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency programme lowered the vaccination age to six months from nine. "No health worker came to tell us," her father said. In May, Health Minister Sardar Md. Sakhawat Husain said the emergency drive had brought cases in hotspots "almost to zero" and the outbreak was under control. Yet in September, Bangladesh reported a daily average of 1,198 new cases of measles, which causes a high fever, cough and telltale rash. That was the highest total since May. The Bangladesh outbreak comes as vaccine hesitancy is rising, particularly in wealthier nations, amid skepticism championed by figures such as US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In Bangladesh, access to inoculations and awareness are bigger hurdles, experts said. Until recently, Bangladesh had been a vaccination success story. The WHO and the United Nations children’s agency UNICEF estimated that in 2024 it achieved 96% coverage for the first vaccine dose and 93% for the second, which is given to capture the small percentage of children who don't develop immunity after one shot. But that same year, protests erupted that ended 15 years of rule by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. In the ensuing political turmoil, health workers went on strike, vaccine orders were delayed and follow-up vaccinations that usually accompany routine programmes were disrupted. Nadia Akter Manna, the mother of Labiba Akter, shows a few personal items bought for her daughter before she died. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain Humayun Rashid, the father of Labiba Akter, works on his carpentry in September, three months after his daughter's death. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90%, while second-dose coverage was 86%, several percentage points below the 95% needed for herd immunity. The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025. It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100% of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers. EMERGENCY PROGRAMME MISSED MILLIONS Still, when the measles outbreak erupted, Bangladesh responded swiftly and initially seemed to be winning the battle. An emergency programme was followed by an initial slowdown in new cases after almost 20 million children received a vaccination in April and May. The government said it had covered every child in the target age group of six months to five years. But in reality the programme fell short. This emerged when another routine health intervention in June had a target list with 4 million more children than the measles campaign despite covering the same age group. "There is a gap," prime ministerial adviser Hyder told Reuters on September 14, as measles cases rose again, blaming vaccine hesitancy by parents or child illnesses for keeping kids away. Iqbal and Sharmin wait as their five-month-old son, Esa, receives treatment for measles in the neonatal intensive care unit of a hospital in Narayanganj, Bangladesh, May 11, 2026. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain Other challenges have also emerged. Documents detailing meetings in April and August between the government, the WHO and other health partners, reviewed by Reuters and not previously reported, show how efforts to act fast may have led to shortcomings. Minutes from the April 19 meeting outlined how the government opted for just one round of so-called readiness checks before launching its emergency vaccination programme due to time constraints, instead of the typical four rounds. Checks cover everything from ensuring fridges are available for keeping vaccines cool to determining how many children should be vaccinated. The single round of checks suggested most - but not all - districts were ready, according to the minutes. Eight-year-old Masum receives treatment in the overcrowded measles isolation ward of Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital in Sylhet, one of the worst-hit areas in Bangladesh's measles outbreak. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain The 100-bed Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital in the Sylhet region has been overwhelmed by measles cases. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain On the day Reuters visited the hospital in September, 178 patients were admitted. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain THE POOREST ‘PAY THE PRICE’ "When preparedness checks are not done properly, it is often the poorest and hardest-to-reach children who miss out on vaccination and pay the price," said Professor Mahmudur Rahman, an epidemiologist and chair of Bangladesh's National Verification Committee for Measles and Rubella Elimination. Hyder said the April campaign was launched in four weeks. Yet Tajul Islam Abdul Bari, who led immunisation in Bangladesh until 2017, said campaigns usually demand months of planning. By the August meeting, shortcomings in the rollout were identified. Minutes noted the proportion of children with confirmed measles cases who had not been vaccinated was "virtually unchanged between pre-campaign (82%) and post-campaign (85%) ... underscoring persistent coverage gaps". The WHO did not respond to questions about the April and August meetings. But deputy WHO representative to Bangladesh, Dr Rajesh Narwal, said the WHO was determined to support the government in its goal of vaccinating every child at risk. "Routine immunisation must become more effective and resilient so that these gaps do not develop again," he said. In Sylhet, where official records show 180 children have died, 8 of 16 families Reuters interviewed in September said they had not seen health workers offering vaccinations. At least six families said health workers visited only after a child had died from measles in their community. A measles survivor, two-year-old Al Raiyan Twoha sleeps on his mother Rajia Begum's shoulder in the Sylhet region of Bangladesh. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain At the end of September, the government launched a new campaign to target 3.4 million children previously missed. "We will involve people across villages so that no child is left behind," the health minister told a news conference. Yet reaching every child remains a challenge. UNICEF and the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics say as many as 40% of children go unregistered, while government data showed around a third of health worker posts are unfilled. Health experts are also pushing the government to expand the programme to vaccinate children over five. That age group represents a third of measles cases, the WHO says. In addition, scientists in Bangladesh are studying why immunity is waning faster than expected in babies up to six months or so. They are usually still protected by maternal antibodies, experts say. Ensuring prompt medical care is vital, the WHO says, another challenge for Bangladesh as it also fights a dengue epidemic . In September, every ward in Sylhet's 100-bed Shahid Shamsuddin Ahmed Hospital, which is treating measles, appeared overwhelmed. On the day Reuters visited, 178 patients were admitted. The blue dress of measles victim Labiba Akter hangs on a line in the village in Bangladesh’s Sylhet region where her parents live. REUTERS/Mohammad Ponir Hossain

item.title: 海外勢の米国債保有、8月は9.33兆ドルに増加 英加がけん引
item.description: [ニューヨーク １６日 ロイター] - 米財務省が１６日発表した８月の対米証券投資統計によると、海外勢の米国債保有残...
item.dc:creator: ロイター
item.content:encoded:
海外勢の米国債保有、8月は9.33兆ドルに増加　英加がけん引 10/17 6:34 配信

米ドル紙幣。３月撮影。REUTERS/Dado Ruvic

[ニューヨーク １６日 ロイター] - 米財務省が１６日発表した８月の対米証券投資統計によると、海外勢の米国債保有残高は９兆３３１０億ドルと、前月の９兆２４８０億ドルから増加した。２カ月連続の減少から増加に転じた。英国とカナダの保有が増加をけん引した。

前年同月比では１％弱の増加にとどまった。

日本の保有高は８月に１兆０６８０億ドルと、７月の１兆１０３０億ドルから３．２％減少し、４カ月連続の減少となった。ただ、日本は海外勢としては依然として米国債の最大保有国だ。保有額は２０２１年１１月に１兆３２５０億ドルでピークを付けた。

海外勢の保有額で２位の英国は、８月の保有高が前月の９９８３億ドルから１．１％増の１兆００９０億ドルとなり、初めて１兆ドルの大台を突破した。

中国の保有高は５９０７億ドルと、７月の６１８０億ドルから２．４％減少し、２００８年８月以来の低水準となった。減少は３カ月連続となった。中国は海外勢の保有額で依然として３位だが、８月の保有額は前年比で約１６％減少した。

米国債は１０８９億ドルの買い越しとなった。７月は３６億ドルの売り越しだった。

米社債は４１６億ドルの買い越しとなり、前月の２６９億ドルから増加した。

対米証券投資は１９９８億ドルの買い越し。前月の８７４億ドルから増加した。
